overview: The Yamato period covers the rise of a single Japanese state from the chiefdoms of the Kofun age. Great keyhole-shaped tombs mark the power of the early rulers; in the sixth and seventh centuries the court took Buddhism, writing and Chinese-style government from Korea and China.

items.text: Keyhole-shaped kofun mounds for rulers; the largest, the Daisen Kofun near Osaka, is 486 meters long.
Haniwa clay figures of warriors, horses, houses and dancers stood on the mounds.
Bronze mirrors, iron swords and gilt-bronze horse trappings came from Korea and China and were buried with the chiefs.
Buddhism arrived from Baekje, and the Soga and Mononobe clans fought over whether to accept it.
Prince Shotoku's Seventeen-Article Constitution set out Buddhist and Confucian principles for officials.
Native kami worship, later called Shinto, continued alongside Buddhism and Confucian learning.
Iron tools and weapons improved through smiths and ore from the Korean kingdoms.
Chinese writing was adopted for court records; the inscribed sword from Inariyama, dated to 471, is among the earliest texts written in Japan.
The Taika Reform began to remodel the court and its land system on Tang lines.
The imperial line that emerged in this period continues to the present.
The Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group was listed by UNESCO.

fall.text: The court moved to a permanent capital at Heijo-kyo in 710, the start of the Nara period.
